title: Conjugation incidence: proper quotient gives closed saturation, finite fixed cosets give density
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type over $k$ [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and all subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Let $G$ be smooth and connected. Let $H\subseteq G$ be smooth and connected. Let $X=G/H$ be the separated finite-type quotient with its left $G$-action and $(G/H)(k)=G(k)/H(k)$, as in [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry]. Put
$$S_H=\{ghg^{-1}:g\in G(k),\ h\in H(k)\}\subseteq G(k).$$
If $X$ is proper over $k$ [def-weil-proper-morphism], there is a Zariski closed subset $Z\subseteq |G|$ with $S_H=Z(k)$, where $Z(k)$ denotes the rational points of $G$ whose underlying points belong to $Z$. If there exists $h_0\in H(k)$ for which
$$\{x\in X(k):h_0x=x\}$$
is finite, there exists a nonempty Zariski open subscheme $V\subseteq G$ [def-weil-open-immersion] such that $V(k)\subseteq S_H$. The second assertion does not require properness of $X$.

source.place: Lemma 17.32(a),(b), printed pp.361--362, including the conjugation incidence subset in (G/H) times G; the statements are expressed on rational points to distinguish them from the underlying scheme points.

proof.text: Write $q:G\to X$. Define the incidence scheme $I\subseteq X\times_kG$ by $a\cdot x=x$: pull back $\Delta_X:X\to X\times_kX$ along $(x,a)\mapsto(a\cdot x,x)$. Since $X$ is separated, its diagonal is a closed immersion, and base change preserves closed immersions. Thus $I$ is closed in $X\times_kG$. Products of finite-type schemes are finite type by base change and composition; a closed immersion is proper, hence finite type. Consequently $I$ is finite type over $k$. Write $p:I\to G$ and $t:I\to X$ for its projections. The local finite-type cancellation clause of the same permanence node also makes $p:I\to G$ locally of finite type, since $I\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is finite type.

source.place: Lemma 17.32, printed p.361: closed incidence subset S, realized by the diagonal.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry], $q$ is faithfully flat, hence flat and surjective, $q(gh)=q(g)$, and $(g,h)\mapsto(g,gh)$ is an isomorphism $G\times_kH\simeq G\times_XG$. Evaluated on $T$-points this says: $q(u)=q(v)$ exactly when $u^{-1}v\in H(T)$. Since $G\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is of finite type, $q$ is locally of finite type by the cancellation clause (f) of [lem-weil-pbc-proper-fp-permanence]. The field $k$ is a Noetherian ring, so $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is Noetherian and the finite-type $k$-scheme $X$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian]; hence $q$ is locally of finite presentation by [pqf-lem-lft-fp-locnoeth]. There is an isomorphism $G\times_kH\simeq I\times_XG$, sending $(g,h)$ to $((q(g),ghg^{-1}),g)$. Its inverse sends $((x,a),g)$ to $(g,g^{-1}ag)$: $q(g)=x$ and $a x=x$ imply $q(ag)=q(g)$, so $g^{-1}ag\in H$. The displayed formulas are mutually inverse morphisms on all test schemes by the quotient criterion and fibre-product universal property. Hence $r:G\times H\to I$, $(g,h)\mapsto(q(g),ghg^{-1})$, is a pullback of $q$. The singleton $\{q\}$ is an fppf covering of schemes [def-pc-fppf-site], hence fppf in the sense of [lem-sfb-space-fppf-covering-calculus] by its clause (4); by clause (2) its pullback $\{r\}$ is fppf, and by (4) again an fppf covering of schemes. Thus $r$ is flat, surjective and locally finitely presented. Moreover $p\circ r=c$ for the conjugation morphism $c(g,h)=ghg^{-1}$, and $p(|I|)=c(|G\times H|)$.

source.place: Lemma 17.32, printed p.361: conjugation and quotient maps; expanded incidence pullback.

proof.text: Connectedness identifies $G$ and $H$ with their identity components, which are geometrically irreducible by the identity-component theorem. The product theorem makes $G\times H$ irreducible. Surjectivity of $r$ then makes $I$ irreducible: pull back any decomposition into two closed subsets to the irreducible source. Both are nonempty, containing the identity pair or its image. The identity-component theorem also gives integral $G_{\mathrm{red}}$ and $H_{\mathrm{red}}$ with the same underlying topologies as $G,H$. They are spectra of the reduced affine coordinate algebras. The finite-type-domain dimension theorem makes $\dim G$ and $\dim H$ finite natural numbers. No reducedness of $I$ is asserted.

source.place: Lemma 17.32(b), printed pp.361--362: irreducibility and finite dimensions in dim S = dim G.

proof.text: At $u=(1,1)\in G\times H$ put $z=r(u)=(q(1),1)$. The fibre $r^{-1}(z)$ is isomorphic to $H$: the equations are $q(g)=q(1)$ and $ghg^{-1}=1$, equivalent on every test scheme to $g\in H$ and $h=1$. The inverse morphisms are $g\mapsto(g,1)$ and first projection. Apply flat composite fibre-dimension additivity to $G\times H\xrightarrow r I\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ at $u$. Both maps are locally of finite type; $r$ is even locally finitely presented. We get $\dim_u(G\times H)=\dim_1H+\dim_zI$. For irreducible locally finite-type schemes the cited local topological dimension equals global dimension. Product dimension therefore gives $\dim G+\dim H=\dim H+\dim I$. Cancelling the finite $\dim H$ yields $\dim I=\dim G$.

source.place: Lemma 17.32(b), printed p.362: expand dim S = dim G using flat dimension additivity.

proof.text: For $a\in G(k)$, the fibre $I_a=I\times_G\operatorname{Spec}k$ along $a$ is also the base change of the closed immersion $I\to X\times_kG$ along $X\simeq X\times_k\operatorname{Spec}k\xrightarrow{1\times a}X\times_kG$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. By clauses (b),(c) of [lem-weil-pbc-proper-fp-permanence] it is a closed subscheme of $X$ whose inclusion is proper, hence of finite type, so $I_a$ is finite type over $k$ by composition [lem-sfb-finite-type-composition-base-change](1). Its $k$-points are $I_a(k)=\{x\in X(k):a x=x\}$. If the underlying point of $a$ belongs to $p(|I|)$, the fibre $I_a$ is nonempty. The Jacobson-space theorem makes its closed points dense, and the residue-field theorem makes every closed point $k$-rational. Thus there is $x\in I_a(k)$. Lift $x$ to $g\in G(k)$ by the quotient theorem [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry]. The equality $q(ag)=q(g)$ and the coset criterion of step 2 give $h=g^{-1}ag\in H(k)$ and $a=ghg^{-1}$. Conversely $ghg^{-1}$ fixes $q(g)$ and therefore lies in the incidence image. This proves $\{a\in G(k):|a|\in p(|I|)\}=S_H$. Properness is not needed.

source.place: Lemma 17.32(a),(b), printed pp.361--362: incidence image equals saturation, with rational-point lifting explicit.

proof.text: If $X$ is proper over $k$, its universal closedness says exactly that $X\times_kG\to G$ is a closed map. As $I$ is closed in $X\times_kG$, $Z=p(|I|)$ is closed in $|G|$. Step 5 gives $Z(k)=S_H$, proving the first assertion.

source.place: Lemma 17.32(a), printed p.361: closed projection from a complete quotient.

proof.text: Let $h_0\in H(k)$ have finitely many fixed points in $X(k)$. The finite-type fibre $F=I_{h_0}$ has exactly those rational points, hence $F(k)$ is finite. It is nonempty because $q(1)$ is fixed by $H$. Its closed points are dense by the Jacobson-space theorem and are $k$-rational by the residue-field theorem. They form a finite set of closed points, which is itself closed, so density implies that they exhaust $|F|$. Every point of this finite space is closed; its nonempty irreducible closed subsets are singletons. Thus $\dim F=0$, in particular its local topological dimension at $(q(1),h_0)$ is zero. This holds even if $F$ is nonreduced.

source.place: Lemma 17.32(b), printed pp.361--362: finite fixed-point fibre has dimension zero.

proof.text: Apply the irreducible fibre-dimension lower bound to $p:I\to G$, with irreducible finite-type source and finite-type target by steps 1 and 3. It gives a natural number $e$ with $\dim I=\dim\overline{p(|I|)}+e$, and every local fibre dimension at least $e$. Step 7 forces $e=0$, and step 4 gives $\dim\overline{p(|I|)}=\dim G$. The identity-component theorem gives an integral affine $G_{\mathrm{red}}$ with the topology and dimension of $G$. A proper closed subset of this irreducible affine variety has dimension at most $\dim G-1$ by affine dimension drop. Thus the nonempty closed subset $\overline{p(|I|)}$ cannot be proper; it equals $|G|$. The incidence image is dense.

source.place: Lemma 17.32(b), printed p.362: A.72 and dominance of the incidence projection.

proof.text: For $c:G\times_kH\to G$ from step 2, the affine fibre-product theorem writes the source as $\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_kB)$ when $G=\operatorname{Spec}A$ and $H=\operatorname{Spec}B$. This source is finite type by finite-type base change and composition; the target is affine finite type too. Affine Chevalley therefore makes $c(|G\times H|)=p(|I|)$ constructible. By step 8 it is dense, so the constructible-open theorem supplies a nonempty open subset $V\subseteq |G|$ contained in it. Give $V$ its open-subscheme structure. For each $a\in V(k)$, step 5 implies $a\in S_H$. Therefore $V(k)\subseteq S_H$. Properness was used only in step 6, so the second assertion is independent of it.

source.place: Lemma 17.32(b), printed p.362: A.15 and the nonempty open in the constructible image.

proof_origin.place: Lemma 17.32(a),(b), printed pp.361--362; expanded incidence pullback, dimension equality, and rational image identification.
